bull_bear.body:
- Integrated plantation-to-manufacturing model with no bought-leaf purchase at any factory, giving complete control over the cultivation and manufacturing process and supporting quality, traceability and integrity
- Estates concentrated in the South Bank of Upper Assam, a region renowned for producing high-quality Assam teas
- Product acceptance in both the Indian domestic market and with prominent importers in Germany, UK, USA and the Middle East
- Dual route to market — teas sold through auction as well as private channels, ensuring broad market access
- Large, settled plantation workforce (over 3,538 personnel at estates and other establishments as on 31st March 2026) with cordial industrial relations across all estates and welfare provision (housing, healthcare, education, provident fund, gratuity)
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Climate and weather dependence — erratic rainfall and fluctuating ambient temperatures across North East tea-growing regions — MD&A Risks & Concerns states the tea industry is largely dependent on climatic conditions, with weather patterns playing a critical role in determining overall production; erratic rainfall and temperature swings have become increasingly frequent and adversely affect crop yields, particularly during the peak harvesting season. The Outlook section adds that industry viability continues to be impacted by the escalating impact of extreme climatic conditions, and Opportunities & Threats flags vulnerability to climate change and global warming affecting both yield and quality.
- Rising pest incidence raising crop-protection cost — Fluctuating temperature levels have resulted in the growth and proliferation of pests, thereby increasing the cost of crop protection — a direct, recurring cost headwind on an unhedgeable input.
- Labour availability in a labour-intensive plantation model — Tea cultivation faces significant challenges from labour availability during peak seasons; any shortage may adversely affect timely plucking, impacting crop quality and crop productivity. The Company employed over 3,538 personnel at its estates and other establishments as on 31st March 2026, so labour is both the key operating input and the key fixed cost.
- Cost escalation outpacing realisations — wages plus gas, electricity, fuel, pesticides and fertilizers — Opportunities & Threats names selling prices that fail to keep pace with rising costs as the industry's key challenge, and the Outlook states profitability is likely to be impacted due to escalation in salaries, wages and other input costs, leading to an increase in overall cost. With no pass-through mechanism at auction, this compresses margin directly.
- Price volatility and demand-supply sensitivity of the tea market — The tea market is highly sensitive to fluctuations of demand and supply, weather conditions, quality differentials and the intensity of international competition; industry viability is impacted by volatile market dynamics. Teas are sold through auction or private channels, leaving realisations exposed to market clearing prices.
- Single-segment, single-crop concentration — The Company operates in a single segment business — cultivation and manufacture of CTC and orthodox teas — with no change in the nature of business during the year and continued concentration on the core tea business. There is no diversification to absorb a bad crop year or a price downcycle.
- Geographic concentration in the South Bank of Upper Assam — All four tea estates are located in the South Bank of Upper Assam, so a single regional weather, pest or labour event affects the entire asset base simultaneously; the report itself notes that North India (Assam and North Bengal) accounts for approximately 83% of the country's total tea production, making the regional exposure structural rather than diversifiable.
- Export-market access and trade barriers, plus international competition — Teas are sold to prominent importers in Germany, UK, USA and the Middle East, and management states sustained efforts are being made to identify and mitigate trade barriers; the Outlook also names the intensity of international competition as a sensitivity for the market.

outlook.body: The annual report discloses no expansion, capacity-addition or new-project programme. The Company continues to operate four tea estates on the South Bank of Upper Assam under an integrated plantation-to-manufacturing model, with no bought leaf processed at any of its factories, and states there has been no change in the nature of business during the year. The only forward-looking operating intent expressed is organic — enhancing turnover through continuous improvement in tea yield, quality and operational efficiency, and producing premium-quality teas cost-efficiently by leveraging innovative agricultural and manufacturing practices. outlook.body:
- Outlook for the tea industry remains positive, driven by evolving consumer preferences, growing demand and continued improvements in the country's distribution infrastructure
- Tea demand is robust across both domestic and international markets; Indian tea consumption has increased in recent years due to its health benefits
- The Indian tea industry has expanded and diversified its portfolio with a wide range of tea varieties, blends and value-added offerings, creating new growth opportunities domestically and internationally
- Global tea production and consumption have shown a consistent upward trend; global production rose to approximately 7,266 million kilograms in 2025 from 7,087 million kilograms in 2024, with India at approximately 1,370 million kilograms versus 1,304 million kilograms
- North India (Assam and North Bengal) produces approximately 83% of the country's total tea production — the Company's four estates sit in this belt
- Margin headwind: selling prices fail to keep pace with rising costs — escalation of salaries and wages and input costs such as gas, electricity, fuel, pesticides and fertilizers — and profitability is likely to be impacted by this cost escalation
- Volume/quality risk: the tea market is highly sensitive to demand-supply fluctuations, weather conditions, quality differentials and the intensity of international competition, and viability is impacted by volatile market dynamics and the escalating impact of extreme climatic conditions
